core_obligations: Translate membership in the kernel into equations (proof lines 9700-9703): with a basis v_1, ..., v_n of V and F(v_i) = sum a_ij v_j, a vector v = sum lambda_i v_i lies in the kernel of F - 1 if and only if the equations sum lambda_i^p a_ij = lambda_j hold for all j.

Identify the solutions with the points of a finite closed subscheme (proof lines 9703-9705): by the companion lemma these equations cut out a closed subscheme Z of affine n-space over k which is finite over Spec(k).
Conclude by base change (proof lines 9705-9706): for the extension k'/k of algebraically closed fields one has Z(k) = Z(k'), so the kernel of F - 1 maps isomorphically onto the kernel of F' - 1.
proof_roadmap: Choose a basis and rewrite membership in the kernel as a system of Frobenius-linear equations.
Use the companion lemma to see that the solution set is the set of k-points of a closed subscheme of affine space finite over Spec(k).
Observe that the set of points does not change under an extension of algebraically closed fields and conclude the isomorphism of kernels.
difficulty_reason: The lemma is stated inside the situation of the preceding Frobenius linear lemma and asserts that extending the algebraically closed base field does not change the kernel of F - 1 (statement lines 9691-9697). The proof writes the kernel out in coordinates: after choosing a basis the condition becomes a system of Frobenius-linear equations (proof lines 9700-9703), which by the companion lemma cut out a closed subscheme of affine space finite over Spec(k) (proof lines 9703-9705); the conclusion then follows from the equality of the point sets over k and over k' (proof lines 9705-9706). The non-formal content is the coordinate description and its interpretation as a finite closed subscheme. The claim is H1: one coordinate computation fed into a named companion result.
